INDUSTRIAL HOMEWORK: MANUFACTURE IN THE WORKER’S OWN HOME (LAB. CODE §§ 2650–2667) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme Manufacturing, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California statutory law says about industrial homework — manufacturing work performed in a worker's own dwelling for an employer. That subject is governed by Part 10 of Division 2 of the Labor Code, headed "INDUSTRIAL HOMEWORK" and running from section 2650 through section 2667. The activity Acme Manufacturing, Inc. has described for the purposes of this sheet is: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

Almost every other information sheet in this corpus about the period during employment assumes a workplace the employer controls: the injury and illness prevention program, the heat and wildfire-smoke standards, the noise and bloodborne-pathogen standards, the emergency action plan, the suitable-seating requirement, exit searches and employer-controlled time, and workplace video surveillance all take as given a place of business the employer owns or occupies. The domestic-worker material takes as given a household, but somebody else's household. Part 10 addresses the remaining case: the article is made inside the worker's own home, and the employer may never set foot there.

The scheme Part 10 sets up has three moving parts. Some manufacture in a home is flatly unlawful no matter who holds what paper. The rest is lawful only if the employer holds a state licence and the worker holds a state permit. Failure at either end is a misdemeanour, and the goods themselves can be seized.

This sheet states what the statutes say. It does not determine whether any particular task, arrangement, dwelling, article or industry falls inside or outside any of these sections, does not evaluate anything Acme Manufacturing, Inc. or any worker has done, and does not predict how any agency or court would treat any arrangement.

WHERE PART 10 SITS IN THE LABOR CODE, AND HOW BROADLY IT DEFINES ITS TERMS
The Legislative Counsel's publication prints Part 10 under the heading "PART 10. INDUSTRIAL HOMEWORK [2650 - 2667]" with the note "( Part 10 added by Stats. 1939, Ch. 809. )", inside Division 2 of the Labor Code, "EMPLOYMENT REGULATION AND SUPERVISION [200 - 2699.8]". The part immediately following it is "PART 11. GARMENT MANUFACTURING [2670 - 2693.1]", added by Statutes of 1980, chapter 633 — the registration, recordkeeping and brand-guarantor scheme this corpus treats separately. The two parts are adjacent and govern overlapping ground.

Section 2650 is the definitional section, and each of its definitions is written wide. "To manufacture" is not confined to making a thing: it reaches finishing, assembling, inspecting, wrapping and packaging. "Home" is defined by dwelling rather than by ownership, extends to the most extensive premises used in whole or in part as a dwelling, and takes in outbuildings under the control of the person dwelling there. "Industrial homework" is any manufacture in a home of materials or articles for an employer, unless the articles are for the personal use of the employer or the employer's family. "Employer" reaches a person who employs a homeworker indirectly or through an independent contractor. And "to employ" is defined to include mere toleration: suffering or permitting articles under one's custody or control to be manufactured in a home. "Division" throughout the part means the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement.

THE ARTICLES THAT MAY NOT BE MADE IN A HOME AT ALL, AND THE LICENCE THAT CANNOT AUTHORIZE THEM
Section 2651 does not regulate the manufacture of certain articles by homework. It forbids it. The section names food and drink; articles for use in connection with the serving of food or drink; articles of wearing apparel; toys and dolls; tobacco; drugs and poisons; bandages and other sanitary goods; and explosives, fireworks and articles of like character. Wearing apparel — the industry Part 11 of the same division regulates through registration — is on that list.

Two features of the section carry weight beyond the list. First, the prohibition is stated to override the permission system that the rest of the part builds: the section says in terms that no licence or permit issued under the part shall be deemed to authorize such manufacture. A licensed employer and a permitted homeworker are, on the face of the section, no better placed than an unlicensed one as to a listed article. Second, the list does not close. Its final item is not a class of article at all but a standard the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement applies: articles whose manufacture by industrial homework the division determines to be injurious to the health or welfare of homeworkers in the industry, or to render unduly difficult the maintenance of existing labor standards or the enforcement of labor standards established by law or regulation for factory workers in the industry. The comparator written into that standard is the factory worker.

HOW AN ENTIRE INDUSTRY CAN BE CLOSED TO HOMEWORK: INVESTIGATION, ORDER, AND A HEARING THAT COMES AFTERWARDS
Beyond the fixed list in section 2651, the division may shut homework out of a whole industry. Section 2652 gives it the power to investigate an industry employing homeworkers to determine whether the wages and conditions of employment of those homeworkers are injurious to their health and welfare, or have the effect of rendering unduly difficult the maintenance or enforcement of labor standards established for factory workers in the industry. Section 2653 supplies the investigative machinery, giving the division the powers that Article 2 (commencing with section 11180) of chapter 2, part 1, division 3, title 2 of the Government Code gives to the head of a department.

Section 2654 is where the order issues. On the basis of information in its possession, with or without an investigation, if the division finds that homework cannot continue in an industry without the stated injury, it shall by order declare such industrial homework to be unlawful and require all employers in the industry to discontinue manufacture by industrial homework. The order must set out the types of manufacturing prohibited after its effective date.

The hearing follows the order rather than preceding it. Section 2655 opens with the words "After making such order", and then requires a public hearing at which employers, homeworkers, their representatives and any other interested person may be heard, with public notice at least 30 days before the hearing and written notice to every business and employer the division believes may be adversely affected.

THE EMPLOYER'S INDUSTRIAL HOMEWORK LICENCE: FEE PER WORKER, ONE YEAR, NOT TRANSFERABLE
Where the industry is not one section 2651 prohibits, homework is lawful only through a licence. Section 2658, subdivision (a), states the requirement as a prohibition on the employer: a person shall not employ an industrial homeworker in any industry not prohibited by section 2651 unless that person has obtained a valid industrial homework licence from the division. Because section 2650 defines "to employ" to include tolerating or permitting articles under one's custody or control to be manufactured in a home, the licensing duty attaches to arrangements that do not look like direct hiring.

The fee is charged per worker, not per business: subdivision (b) sets a licence fee of one hundred dollars for each industrial homeworker employed, and makes the licence valid for one year from issuance unless sooner revoked or suspended. Renewal is at the same rate and conditions. Subdivision (d) lets the division revoke or suspend on a finding that the licensee has violated the part, or failed to comply with the division's regulations or with the licence, and states that the licence is not transferable. Subdivision (e), added when the section was last amended in 2016, directs all licence and permit fees received under the part into the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund.

THE WORKER'S OWN PERMIT: TIED TO ONE EMPLOYER, TO ONE DWELLING, AND TO THAT EMPLOYER'S LICENCE
The permission runs in both directions. Section 2660 forbids any person to do industrial homework in this state without a valid homeworker's permit in his possession, sets the fee at twenty-five dollars, and makes the permit valid for work done for the licensed employer named in it, for one year. Two further limits sit in the same section: the permit is valid only for work performed by the applicant himself in his own home, so it does not cover another member of the household; and the division may waive the fee where the applicant asks and can establish that paying it would cause financial hardship. Section 2659 closes the circuit from the other side, forbidding any person to engage, suffer or permit homework, or to tolerate articles under his custody or control to be manufactured by homework, by a person not holding either a valid employer's licence or a homeworker's permit.

Section 2661 states who may not receive a permit, and the grounds reach the applicant's health and the applicant's dwelling as well as the applicant's age: no permit shall issue to a person under 16 years of age, to a person suffering from an infectious, contagious or communicable disease, or to a person living in a home that is not clean, sanitary and free from such disease.

Section 2662 makes the permit dependent on the employer. The division may revoke or suspend a permit on a finding that the homeworker is working contrary to the permit's conditions or in violation of the part, or has let a person without a permit assist him — and also on expiration or revocation of the industrial homework licence of the employer. On the face of the section the worker's authorization falls with the employer's, without regard to anything the worker has done.

CRIMINAL EXPOSURE ON THE EMPLOYER SIDE: GRADUATED FINES, A NEGLIGENCE OFFENCE, A PRESUMPTION, AND SUSPENSION OF THE BUSINESS LICENCE
Part 10 is enforced through the criminal law. Section 2658.5 is the principal provision, and it is drafted to reach up the supply chain: the word "person" in that section is expressly deemed to include manufacturers, contractors, jobbers and wholesalers. Without a then-valid licence, it is a misdemeanour to employ a homeworker; to tolerate, suffer or permit articles owned by or under one's custody or control to be taken to a home for manufacture by homework; to accept and pay a person for the manufacture in a home of articles by homework; or to place an advertisement for industrial homework whose performance the part does not permit. The penalties escalate by conviction: up to one thousand dollars or 30 days for the first, up to five thousand dollars or six months for the second, and up to thirty thousand dollars or one year for the third and any subsequent conviction. On a third conviction, the section adds a consequence outside the criminal fine — the business licence of the manufacturer or owner of the goods shall be suspended for a period not to exceed three years.

Section 2658.1 creates a separate, lesser offence: an unlicensed person who negligently fails to prevent articles under his custody or control from being taken to a home for manufacture by homework is guilty of a misdemeanour. The same section supplies an evidentiary rule pointing at the factory owner: possession, control or custody of articles for the purpose of homework manufacture by someone other than the owner or operator of a factory is presumptive evidence that the owner or operator negligently failed to prevent it, where it is established that the owner or operator is entitled to possession, control or custody.

Section 2667 supplies the residual offence and extends it to individuals acting for someone else. Unless otherwise provided in the part, every person acting either individually or as an officer, agent, employee or independent contractor for another person who violates or neglects to comply with any provision of the part, or any regulation made under it, is guilty of a misdemeanour. The same section adds that where the part prohibits employing a person in certain work or under certain conditions, the employer shall not knowingly permit that person to work with or without compensation, and gives the Attorney General authority to seek injunctive relief in furtherance of the part's purposes.

THE WORKER IS ALSO PROSECUTABLE — AND IS ALSO GIVEN A USE IMMUNITY FOR WHAT THE WORKER TELLS THE DIVISION
Part 10 does not confine its penalties to employers. Section 2660.5 makes it a misdemeanour for a person to do industrial homework without a valid permit in his possession, punishable by a fine of not more than fifty dollars for the first offence and not more than one hundred dollars for the second. The same section gives the court a suspension power framed in terms of the worker's cooperation: the court may suspend the fine on condition that the homeworker cooperates with the division in the lawful prosecutions of persons violating the part and to secure compliance with it, or on condition that the defendant refrains from any future violation.

Section 2660.1 runs the same theme through the investigative stage and supplies the counterweight. Every person doing industrial homework — the section says expressly, with or without a valid permit — shall reveal to the division on demand the name and address of the employer, the name and address of the owner or source of the articles or materials, and the rate of compensation. The second sentence of the section then bars the division from turning that answer against the worker: the information so revealed shall not be used by the division in any action against or prosecution of the homeworker. The disclosure duty and the use restriction sit in the same section, and the duty is imposed on the unpermitted worker whose very presence in the home is the offence section 2660.5 defines.

THE LABEL: EVERY ARTICLE MADE BY HOMEWORK MUST CARRY THE EMPLOYER'S NAME AND ADDRESS
Section 2663 attaches identification to the goods themselves. No person shall tolerate, suffer or permit materials or articles to be manufactured by industrial homework unless a label or other mark of identification bearing the employer's name and address has been conspicuously affixed to each article or material — or, if that is impossible, to the package or other container in which the goods are kept. The section requires the name and address to be printed or written legibly in English.

The label is what makes the rest of the enforcement scheme operable. It is the mechanism by which goods found in a home, or in transit, can be traced back to the manufacturer, jobber or wholesaler whom section 2658.5 makes criminally liable, and it is the address to which section 2664 directs the division's notice of confiscation.

CONFISCATION OF THE GOODS, THE FIFTEEN-DAY APPEAL, AND THE NOTICE THAT DEPENDS ON A LABEL
Part 10 authorizes the state to take the goods. Section 2664, subdivision (a), lets the division confiscate any article or material being manufactured in a home in violation of any provision of the part. Confiscated articles go into the division's custody, to be destroyed or disposed of under regulations adopted pursuant to section 2666, and the subdivision adds an express restriction on the state's own disposal: the articles shall not enter the mainstream of commerce and shall not be offered for sale. Section 2658.7 adds a separate confiscation power for goods found in the homeworker's home, in transit to or from it, or in the manufacturer's or his contractor's possession, which constitute evidence of a violation, and makes a determination that section 2651 has been violated carry forfeiture of those goods with it. The closing paragraph of section 2658.7 gives the division power to investigate an industry in which homework has been made unlawful by section 2651, to determine compliance.

Section 2664 supplies the only adjudicative track in Part 10. The division must give notice of the confiscation and of the appeal procedure by certified mail. A person contesting the confiscation files a written notice of appeal with the Office of the Labor Commissioner within 15 days after service; the Labor Commissioner must hold a recorded hearing within 30 days of a timely notice; the decision must consist of findings of fact, legal analysis and an order, served by first-class mail within 15 days of the hearing's conclusion; and judicial review is by petition for writ of mandate filed within 45 days of service of the decision. The Labor Commissioner may affirm, modify or dismiss the confiscation and may order the return of none, some or all of the goods.

The notice, however, has only one addressee. Subdivision (a) directs it to the person whose name and address are affixed to the article as provided in the part — that is, to the section 2663 label.

That subject is governed by Part 10 of Division 2 of the Labor Code, headed "INDUSTRIAL HOMEWORK" and running from section 2650 through section 2667. The domestic-worker material takes as given a household, but somebody else's household. Part 10 addresses the remaining case: the article is made inside the worker's own home, and the employer may never set foot there.

The scheme Part 10 sets up has three moving parts. Some manufacture in a home is flatly unlawful no matter who holds what paper. The rest is lawful only if the employer holds a state licence and the worker holds a state permit. Failure at either end is a misdemeanour, and the goods themselves can be seized.

This sheet states what the statutes say. The section names food and drink; articles for use in connection with the serving of food or drink; articles of wearing apparel; toys and dolls; tobacco; drugs and poisons; bandages and other sanitary goods; and explosives, fireworks and articles of like character. Beyond the fixed list in section 2651, the division may shut homework out of a whole industry. Section 2652 gives it the power to investigate an industry employing homeworkers to determine whether the wages and conditions of employment of those homeworkers are injurious to their health and welfare, or have the effect of rendering unduly difficult the maintenance or enforcement of labor standards established for factory workers in the industry. Part 10 is enforced through the criminal law. Section 2658.5 is the principal provision, and it is drafted to reach up the supply chain: the word "person" in that section is expressly deemed to include manufacturers, contractors, jobbers and wholesalers. Without a then-valid licence, it is a misdemeanour to employ a homeworker; to tolerate, suffer or permit articles owned by or under one's custody or control to be taken to a home for manufacture by homework; to accept and pay a person for the manufacture in a home of articles by homework; or to place an advertisement for industrial homework whose performance the part does not permit. The penalties escalate by conviction: up to one thousand dollars or 30 days for the first, up to five thousand dollars or six months for the second, and up to thirty thousand dollars or one year for the third and any subsequent conviction. On a third conviction, the section adds a consequence outside the criminal fine — the business licence of the manufacturer or owner of the goods shall be suspended for a period not to exceed three years.

Section 2658.1 creates a separate, lesser offence: an unlicensed person who negligently fails to prevent articles under his custody or control from being taken to a home for manufacture by homework is guilty of a misdemeanour. The same section supplies an evidentiary rule pointing at the factory owner: possession, control or custody of articles for the purpose of homework manufacture by someone other than the owner or operator of a factory is presumptive evidence that the owner or operator negligently failed to prevent it, where it is established that the owner or operator is entitled to possession, control or custody.

Section 2667 supplies the residual offence and extends it to individuals acting for someone else. Unless otherwise provided in the part, every person acting either individually or as an officer, agent, employee or independent contractor for another person who violates or neglects to comply with any provision of the part, or any regulation made under it, is guilty of a misdemeanour. The same section adds that where the part prohibits employing a person in certain work or under certain conditions, the employer shall not knowingly permit that person to work with or without compensation, and gives the Attorney General authority to seek injunctive relief in furtherance of the part's purposes.

Part 10 does not confine its penalties to employers. Section 2660.5 makes it a misdemeanour for a person to do industrial homework without a valid permit in his possession, punishable by a fine of not more than fifty dollars for the first offence and not more than one hundred dollars for the second. Part 10 authorizes the state to take the goods. Section 2664, subdivision (a), lets the division confiscate any article or material being manufactured in a home in violation of any provision of the part. Confiscated articles go into the division's custody, to be destroyed or disposed of under regulations adopted pursuant to section 2666, and the subdivision adds an express restriction on the state's own disposal: the articles shall not enter the mainstream of commerce and shall not be offered for sale. Section 2658.7 adds a separate confiscation power for goods found in the homeworker's home, in transit to or from it, or in the manufacturer's or his contractor's possession, which constitute evidence of a violation, and makes a determination that section 2651 has been violated carry forfeiture of those goods with it. The closing paragraph of section 2658.7 gives the division power to investigate an industry in which homework has been made unlawful by section 2651, to determine compliance.

Section 2664 supplies the only adjudicative track in Part 10. The division must give notice of the confiscation and of the appeal procedure by certified mail. A person contesting the confiscation files a written notice of appeal with the Office of the Labor Commissioner within 15 days after service; the Labor Commissioner must hold a recorded hearing within 30 days of a timely notice; the decision must consist of findings of fact, legal analysis and an order, served by first-class mail within 15 days of the hearing's conclusion; and judicial review is by petition for writ of mandate filed within 45 days of service of the decision. The Labor Commissioner may affirm, modify or dismiss the confiscation and may order the return of none, some or all of the goods.

The notice, however, has only one addressee. Subdivision (a) directs it to the person whose name and address are affixed to the article as provided in the part — that is, to the section 2663 label.

citations.quote: Any article or material which is being manufactured in a home in violation of any provision of this part may be confiscated by the division. Articles or material confiscated pursuant to this section shall be placed in the custody of the division, which shall be responsible for destroying or disposing of them pursuant to regulations adopted under Section 2666, provided that the articles or material shall not enter the mainstream of commerce and shall not be offered for sale.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the addressee of the notice of confiscation
citations.quote: The division shall, by certified mail, give notice of the confiscation and the procedure for appealing the confiscation to the person whose name and address are affixed to the article or material as provided in this part.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the fifteen-day appeal and the thirty-day hearing
citations.quote: To contest the confiscation of articles or material, a person shall, within 15 days after service of the notice of confiscation, file a written notice of appeal with the Office of the Labor Commissioner at the address that appears on the notice of confiscation. Within 30 days after the timely filing of a notice of appeal, the Labor Commissioner shall hold a hearing on the appeal.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the content of the decision and the route to court
citations.quote: The decision of the Labor Commissioner shall consist of findings of fact, legal analysis, and an order. The decision shall be served by first-class mail on all parties to the hearing, to the last known address of the parties on file with the Labor Commissioner, within 15 days of the conclusion of the hearing. Service shall be complete pursuant to Section 1013 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Judicial review shall be by petition for writ of mandate, filed with the appropriate court, within 45 days of service of the decision.

citations.quote: Any goods, assembled or partially assembled, whether found in the homeworker’s home, in transit to or from the home, or in the manufacturer’s or his contractor’s possession, pursuant to an order obtained under Section 2656, which constitute evidence of a violation of industrial homework laws, shall be confiscated by the division and properly marked and identified.

citations.quote: A determination or decision that a violation of Section 2651 has been committed shall carry with it, in addition to whatever other penalties are imposed as prescribed in this act, forfeiture of the aforementioned confiscated goods, garments or products identified as goods, garments or products produced by illegal industrial homework

Part 10 does not set its own wage rates. Section 2665, subdivision (a), imports the general standards instead: every person who employs or otherwise avails himself of the services of industrial homeworkers in this state shall comply with the labor standards as provided in chapter 1 (commencing with section 1171) of part 4 of division 2 of the Labor Code — the chapter headed "Wages, Hours and Working Conditions" under which the Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders are made. Homework is therefore not a category of work the Labor Code places outside its ordinary wage standards.

Subdivision (b) requires records kept in a manner approved by the division, in five numbered categories. Three of them concern the worker: the full name and home address of each homeworker; the amount and description of materials delivered to each, with the date of delivery and the rate of compensation; and the gross compensation paid to each, with the date of payment. The other two trace the goods in both directions along the chain: the names and addresses of all agents or independent contractors to whom materials were delivered for homework manufacture, with quantity, description and date; and the names and addresses of all manufacturers or independent contractors from whom articles or materials were received for homework, with quantity, description and date of receipt. Subdivision (c) requires the person to furnish the division, at its request, such reports or information as the division requires to carry out the part, verified as the division requests.

citations.quote: Every person who employs or otherwise avails himself of the services of industrial homeworkers in this State shall: (a) Comply with the labor standards as provided in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 1171) of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Labor Code.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the worker-facing records
citations.quote: 1. Full name and home address of each industrial homeworker employed by him; 2. Amount and description of materials delivered to each industrial homeworker employed by him with date of delivery, and rate of compensation; 3. Gross amount of compensation paid to each industrial homeworker employed by him and date of payment;

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the records that trace goods up and down the chain
citations.quote: 4. Names and addresses of all agents or independent contractors to whom he has delivered materials or articles for manufacture by industrial homework together with quantity, description of materials and date of delivery; 5. Names and addresses of all manufacturers or independent contractors from whom he has received articles or materials for industrial homework together with quantity, description of materials and date of receipt.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the duty to furnish verified reports on request
citations.quote: Furnish to the division at its request reports or information which the division requires to carry out the provisions of this part. Such reports and information shall be verified as requested by the division.

The two premises the part concerns are entered on different terms, and the difference is written into the statutes. To reach the home, the division must go to a magistrate. Section 2656 provides that the division may seek a search warrant under the procedures of chapter 3 (commencing with section 1523) of title 12 of part 2 of the Penal Code — the general search warrant chapter — to enable it to have access to, and to inspect, the premises of any industrial homeworker or distributor in this state.

To reach the employer, it need not. Section 2666 provides that every employer shall permit authorized employees of the division free access to his place of business for the purpose of making investigations authorized by the part, and permit them to inspect and copy payroll or other records or documents relating to enforcement, or interview his employees or agents. The same section makes the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement the enforcing agency; authorizes rules and regulations under the Administrative Procedure Act, chapter 3.5 (commencing with section 11340) of part 1 of division 3 of title 2 of the Government Code, and provides that a violation of such a rule is a violation of the part; and confers on every state, county, municipal or other government law enforcement officer who has reason to suspect a violation all the powers of an authorized representative of the Department of Industrial Relations for the investigation of that suspected violation.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the warrant route to a homeworker's premises
citations.quote: The division may seek a search warrant pursuant to the procedures set forth in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 1523) of Title 12 of Part 2 of the Penal Code to enable it to have access to, and to inspect, the premises of any industrial homeworker or distributor in this state.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, free access to the employer's place of business and to its records
citations.quote: Every employer shall permit authorized employees of the division free access to his place of business for the purpose of making investigations authorized by this part or necessary to carry out its provisions and permit them to inspect and copy his payroll or other records or documents relating to the enforcement of this part, or interview his employees or agents.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act and the effect of a rule violation
citations.quote: The division may make, in accordance with the provisions of Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code, such rules and regulations as are reasonably necessary to carry out the provisions of this part. The violation of any such rule or regulation shall be deemed a violation of this part.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, local law enforcement officers given investigative powers
citations.quote: Every law enforcement officer of the state, any county, municipality, or other government entity who has reason to suspect any violation of this part shall have all the powers of an authorized representative of the Department of Industrial Relations, in the investigation of such suspected violation.
